questions.q: What is the nucleophile in the key C–N bond-forming step of Gabriel phthalimide synthesis, and what is its structure?
questions.a: The nucleophile is the potassium salt of phthalimide (phthalimide anion). It has a nitrogen anion delocalized over two carbonyl groups: a five-membered cyclic imide with the negative charge on nitrogen, resonance-stabilized by the two adjacent C=O groups. A wrong answer (e.g., "phthalimide itself" or "KOH") reveals the student does not recognize that deprotonation is essential to generate the nucleophilic nitrogen; they may attempt the alkylation on neutral phthalimide, which is far less reactive.

questions.q: Why does Gabriel synthesis reliably stop at the primary amine and not produce secondary/tertiary amines or quaternary ammonium salts, unlike direct ammonolysis of alkyl halides?
questions.a: In Gabriel synthesis, the nitrogen is part of a cyclic imide (phthalimide). After the single SN2 alkylation, the nitrogen becomes an N-alkylphthalimide. The nitrogen's lone pair is delocalized into two carbonyl groups, making it far less nucleophilic; moreover, the bulky phthaloyl group sterically hinders a second SN2 attack. In direct ammonolysis, the product primary amine (RNH₂) is still a good nucleophile and attacks more alkyl halide, leading to a mixture. A wrong answer (e.g., "because excess ammonia is used") confuses Gabriel with ammonolysis conditions and misses the structural protection principle.

questions.q: A student wants to prepare 2-phenylethanamine (C₆H₅CH₂CH₂NH₂) via Gabriel synthesis. Which alkyl halide should they use, and will the reaction work efficiently? Justify.
questions.a: Use 2-phenylethyl bromide (or chloride), C₆H₅CH₂CH₂Br. This is a primary benzylic halide; the benzylic position undergoes SN2 readily (even enhanced by resonance stabilization of the transition state), so the reaction works well. A wrong choice like benzyl chloride (C₆H₅CH₂Cl) would give phenylmethanamine (benzylamine), not the target; choosing chlorobenzene (aryl halide) would fail because aryl halides do not undergo SN2. An answer that picks the wrong halide or claims chlorobenzene works reveals confusion between alkyl/aryl halides and SN2 reactivity.

questions.q: Compare the hydrolysis step of Gabriel synthesis (alkaline hydrolysis of N-alkylphthalimide) with the hydrolysis of an amide. What is the key structural difference in the substrate that makes phthalimide hydrolysis require more forcing conditions (concentrated NaOH, reflux) than simple amide hydrolysis?
questions.a: N-Alkylphthalimide is a cyclic imide with two carbonyl groups attached to the same nitrogen; hydrolysis must cleave two N–C(O) bonds to release the amine, whereas a simple amide (R–C(O)NH₂) has only one N–C(O) bond. The imide nitrogen is also less basic/more electron-deficient due to two electron-withdrawing carbonyls, making the carbonyl carbons more electrophilic but the overall cleavage of both bonds requires prolonged heating with strong base. A wrong answer that treats it as a normal amide hydrolysis underestimates the reagent strength/time needed and may not account for the dicarboxylate byproduct.

questions.q: Evaluate the following statement: "Gabriel phthalimide synthesis can be used to prepare p-toluidine (4-methylaniline) from p-tolyl chloride." Is it correct? Explain.
questions.a: Incorrect. p-Tolyl chloride is an aryl halide (chlorine attached directly to the benzene ring). Aryl halides do not undergo SN2 reactions under normal conditions because the C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character (resonance) and the ring sterically hinders backside attack. The phthalimide anion cannot displace chloride from an aryl halide. p-Toluidine is instead made by nitration of toluene followed by reduction, or by ammonolysis of p-tolyl halide under high pressure/temperature (not Gabriel). A student who says "yes" confuses benzyl halides (benzylic, SN2 works) with aryl halides (vinylic/aryl, SN2 fails).

questions.q: Design a two-step sequence (starting from a commercially available alkyl halide) to prepare 3-aminopropanenitrile (NC–CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂) using Gabriel synthesis. Show all reagents and intermediates.
questions.a: Step 1: React 3-bromopropanenitrile (BrCH₂CH₂CH₂CN) with potassium phthalimide in ethanol → N-(3-cyanopropyl)phthalimide. Step 2: Alkaline hydrolysis (conc. NaOH, reflux) → 3-aminopropanenitrile + sodium phthalate. The nitrile group survives both steps (stable to SN2 and base hydrolysis of imide). A good answer shows the correct halide, notes that the nitrile is not affected, and writes the hydrolysis products correctly. A poor answer might use a halide that would self-react (e.g., BrCH₂CH₂Br) or forget that hydrolysis gives the diamine precursor.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Gabriel phthalimide synthesis is a laboratory method for preparing pure primary aliphatic amines by reacting the potassium salt of phthalimide with an alkyl halide via SN2 nucleophilic substitution, followed by alkaline hydrolysis (or hydrazinolysis) to liberate the primary amine and regenerate phthalic acid (or ______).

Fill in the blank: Imagine you need to make pure 1-______ (butan-1-amine) in the lab without getting a mixture of secondary/tertiary amines and quaternary salts — a common headache when you simply heat butyl bromide with excess ammonia.
What is Gabriel phthalimide synthesis? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Gabriel phthalimide synthesis is a laboratory method for preparing pure primary aliphatic amines by reacting the potassium salt of phthalimide with an alkyl halide via SN2 nucleophilic substitution, followed by alkaline hydrolysis (or hydrazinolysis) to liberate the primary amine and regenerate phthalic acid (or phthalhydrazide).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Gabriel phthalimide synthesis is a laboratory method for preparing pure primary aliphatic amines by reacting the potassium salt of phthalimide with an alkyl halide via SN______ nucleophilic substitution, followed by alkaline hydrolysis (or hydrazinolysis) to liberate the primary amine and regenerate phthalic acid (or phthalhydrazide).
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Gabriel phthalimide synthesis?
questions.a: Students often think Gabriel synthesis works for *any* primary amine, including aromatic ones like aniline.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can (1) write the complete three-step sequence (phthalimide → K-salt → N-alkylphthalimide → primary amine) with correct reagents and conditions, (2) explain why the method gives only primary amines and avoids over-alkylation, (3) predict whether a given alkyl halide will work (primary > secondary, no tertiary/aryl), and (4).
